2.4. Bias assessment
The risk of bias in the included studies was assessed independently
by two researchers (S.J. Cai and C.H. Wu) using the revised Cochrane

2.6. Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were performed using RStudio (version 4.4.0).
Intervention networks were established by studies that linked three or
more interventions through direct comparisons. Network meta-analysis
allows both direct and indirect comparisons of interventions within
these intervention networks, using a common comparator as the control
defined in this meta-analysis [69–71]. A Bayesian network
meta-analysis was conducted using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods,
using the "BUGSnet" package [72].
The model selection process involved generating leverage value plots
for fixed-effect and random-effect models using the nma.fit() function.
These plots display the corresponding effective number of parameters,
the total residual deviance, and the deviance information criterion
(DIC). The DIC is a standard criterion for Bayesian model selection and
comparison [73]. Based on the DIC values and leverage plots, the
fixed-effect model was chosen when the DIC difference between the two
models was < five; if the DIC difference was ≥five, the random-effect
model with a smaller DIC was selected. To test for inconsistent as­
sumptions, the parameter type = "inconsistency" was applied to the nma.
model() function.
The mean difference (MD) was calculated as the effect size using the
mean and standard deviation (SD) of SBP and DBP between before and
after intervention reported by each included study. In cases where only
the standard error was reported, we applied standard deviation trans­
formations using the formula recommended in the Cochrane Handbook
[74].

3. Result
3.1. Study selection and characteristics
Our search identified 31,483 references, which were reduced to
25,164 studies after removing duplicates. After title and abstract
screening, 24,487 studies were excluded, and a further 610 studies were
removed after a thorough full-text review. Consequently, this network
meta-analysis included 67 eligible studies (Fig. 1) [34–68,76–107],
which compared the effects of 17 types of lifestyle interventions with the
control group. The 17 lifestyle interventions analyzed in this study
included five single-component interventions, seven two-component
combined interventions, three-component combined interventions,
and one four-component combined intervention.
The baseline characteristics of the included studies are summarized
in Table S3. After bias assessment, 10 studies were considered to be at
high risk of bias, 43 studies were considered to be of some concern, and
14 studies were considered to be at low risk of bias (Figs. 2 and S1).
Articles rated as high risk of bias were mainly due to the lack of blinding
in the randomization process and bias in outcome measures.
3.2. Network meta-analysis for SBP outcome
The results of the network meta-analysis for the SBP outcome are
shown in Fig. 3, with network characteristics outlined in Table S4.
Leverage plots shown in Fig. S2 were used to evaluate model fit, and the
random-effects model was considered more appropriate for the SBP
outcome based on the DIC value (DIC = 261.00, Dres = 136.93).
Furthermore, the fit index, as shown in Fig. S3, confirmed that the
consistency assumption was met in our analysis.

In this study, lifestyle interventions were categorized based on the
specific behaviors participants adopted, either individually or in com­
bination. Specifically, Control (CO) was defined as participants who did
not receive any lifestyle intervention and maintained the original habits.
Dietary supplement (DS) was defined as participants received an inter­
vention involving dietary extract or supplement (e.g. Hawthorn green
tea [34], a combination supplement of polyphenol extract and L-citrul­
line [35], black sesame meal capsules [36], red ginseng [37], c12 Pep­
tide [38], ethanolic extract of whole tomato fruit [39], garlic
preparation [40], lavender extract [41], grape seed extract [42], saf­
flower seed extract [43], soursop supplementation [44], fish oil [45],
commercially available combination dietary supplement capsules [46],
water-soluble vitamins [47], Khar-i-khasak [48], Hwangchil–Unripe
Bokbunja extract mixture [49], Aronia berry (poly)phenol supplemen­
tation [50], hibiscus sabdariffa [51], taurine supplementation [52],
Nisha Amalaki Churna [53]). Exercise (EX) was defined as participants
engaged in any form of exercise intervention (e.g., Baduanjin [54],
aerobics exercise [55,56], yoga [57,58], Mat Pilates training [59],
combined aerobic and resistance training [60], resistance band exercise
training [61], arm swing exercise [62,63], lifestyle physical activity
[64], isometric handgrip exercise [65], isometric exercise training [66],
tai chi [67], endurance exercise training [68]). Health education (HE)was
defined as participants received general health advice, including dietary
guidance and exercise recommendations, without a specific interven­
tion. General healthy diet (GHD) was defined as participants received a
specific dietary intervention aimed at lowering blood pressure, not just
dietary guidance, unless it is a specific dietary pattern, such as DASH
(abbreviation of Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension). Psychologi­
cal care (PC) was defined as participants received mental health care and
management. Meditation (ME), Relaxation therapy (RT), and Massage
(MA) were defined according to their original definitions. TEAS was an
abbreviation for transcutaneous electrical stimulation of acupuncture
points. Lifestyle modification (LSM) was defined as a combination of in­
terventions in addition to those described above, including blood pres­
sure monitoring, alcohol restriction, quitting smoking, etc.
2.6. Statistical analysis
All statistical analyses were performed using RStudio (version 4.4.0).
Intervention networks were established by studies that linked three or
more interventions through direct comparisons. Network meta-analysis
allows both direct and indirect comparisons of interventions within
these intervention networks, using a common comparator as the control
defined in this meta-analysis [69–71]. A Bayesian network
meta-analysis was conducted using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods,
using the "BUGSnet" package [72].
The model selection process involved generating leverage value plots
for fixed-effect and random-effect models using the nma.fit() function.
These plots display the corresponding effective number of parameters,
the total residual deviance, and the deviance information criterion
(DIC). The DIC is a standard criterion for Bayesian model selection and
comparison [73]. Based on the DIC values and leverage plots, the
fixed-effect model was chosen when the DIC difference between the two
models was < five; if the DIC difference was ≥five, the random-effect
model with a smaller DIC was selected. To test for inconsistent as­
sumptions, the parameter type = "inconsistency" was applied to the nma.
model() function.
The mean difference (MD) was calculated as the effect size using the
mean and standard deviation (SD) of SBP and DBP between before and
after intervention reported by each included study. In cases where only
the standard error was reported, we applied standard deviation trans­
formations using the formula recommended in the Cochrane Handbook
[74].
To visualize the network structure of all lifestyle interventions, a
network plot was generated for each outcome of interest. Forest plots
were used to visually compare the effect sizes of lifestyle interventions
relative to the control group, expressed as MD with 95 % credible in­
terval (CrI). A heat plot visualized all relative effect estimates from the
network meta-analysis, including potential comparisons. Ranking
probabilities for intervention efficacy were displayed using rankograms
and surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) plots, offering
insights into the relative effectiveness of each intervention for pre­
hypertension management.
Furthermore, both funnel plot and Egger’s test were performed to
assess publication bias, heterogeneity, and asymmetry. If publication
bias was detected, sensitivity analysis was conducted to test the
robustness of the data by excluding studies with a high risk of bias. The
degree of between-study heterogeneity was examined using the size of
the I-square statistic (I2). I2 values of 25 %, 50 %, and 75 %, respectively,
indicate low, medium, and high heterogeneity, respectively [75]. If I2
exceeds 75 %, the source of heterogeneity was investigated with data.
plot() function, and subgroup analyses were performed to account for
the identified sources of heterogeneity.
3. Result
3.1. Study selection and characteristics
Our search identified 31,483 references, which were reduced to
25,164 studies after removing duplicates. After title and abstract
screening, 24,487 studies were excluded, and a further 610 studies were
removed after a thorough full-text review. Consequently, this network
meta-analysis included 67 eligible studies (Fig. 1) [34–68,76–107],
which compared the effects of 17 types of lifestyle interventions with the
control group. The 17 lifestyle interventions analyzed in this study
included five single-component interventions, seven two-component
combined interventions, three-component combined interventions,
and one four-component combined intervention.
The baseline characteristics of the included studies are summarized
in Table S3. After bias assessment, 10 studies were considered to be at
high risk of bias, 43 studies were considered to be of some concern, and
14 studies were considered to be at low risk of bias (Figs. 2 and S1).
Articles rated as high risk of bias were mainly due to the lack of blinding
in the randomization process and bias in outcome measures.

4. Discussion
This network meta-analysis evaluated the comparative effectiveness
of different lifestyle interventions on SBP and DBP in people with pre­
hypertension. A total of 67 RCTs assessing 17 different interventions and
control were included. Our findings showed that DS plus EX was the most
effective lifestyle intervention for reducing SBP, and HE plus ME was the
most effective way for reducing DBP. Additionally, multi-component
lifestyle interventions showed superior efficacy in managing blood
pressure compared with single-component interventions (e.g., DS, EX).
Notably, this study revealed heterogeneity in the blood pressure mea­
surement outcomes across different intervention durations, age groups,
and regions with different economic levels.
Dietary supplements such as omega-3 fatty acids [109,110], nitrate
[111], polyphenols [112], and certain vitamins [113] have been shown
to support cardiovascular health and lower blood pressure. Our analysis
supports their use in the management of prehypertension. The mecha­
nisms may be attributed to improving endothelial function, reducing
oxidative stress, and regulating vascular tone [109,110,114]. Given

4. Discussion
This network meta-analysis evaluated the comparative effectiveness
of different lifestyle interventions on SBP and DBP in people with pre­
hypertension. A total of 67 RCTs assessing 17 different interventions and
control were included. Our findings showed that DS plus EX was the most
effective lifestyle intervention for reducing SBP, and HE plus ME was the
most effective way for reducing DBP. Additionally, multi-component
lifestyle interventions showed superior efficacy in managing blood
pressure compared with single-component interventions (e.g., DS, EX).
Notably, this study revealed heterogeneity in the blood pressure mea­
surement outcomes across different intervention durations, age groups,
and regions with different economic levels.

supports their use in the management of prehypertension. The mecha­
nisms may be attributed to improving endothelial function, reducing
oxidative stress, and regulating vascular tone [109,110,114]. Given
their ease of use and strong evidence, dietary supplements could be a
practical strategy for the prevention of prehypertension. However, it is
crucial to assess the efficacy of different types of supplements individ­
ually, as responses may vary in different populations. Beyond individual
nutrients, overall dietary patterns such as the DASH diet-which em­
phasizes fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy products, fish, nuts, legumes,
and reduced sodium intake-have been consistently shown to lower blood
pressure [115–117]. Previous systematic reviews have reported that

5. Conclusion
This network meta-analysis evaluated the effectiveness of different
lifestyle interventions in the management of prehypertension. Our re­
sults suggest that DS plus EX was the most effective lifestyle intervention
for reducing SBP in individuals with prehypertension, and HE plus ME
was the most effective lifestyle intervention for reducing DBP. This study
underlines the importance of dietary factors and exercise in the man­
agement of prehypertension and highlights the superiority of multi-
component lifestyle interventions. Furthermore, tailored approaches
are essential to address the increasing burden of prehypertension in
different populations.

5. Conclusion
This network meta-analysis evaluated the effectiveness of different
lifestyle interventions in the management of prehypertension. Our re­
sults suggest that DS plus EX was the most effective lifestyle intervention
for reducing SBP in individuals with prehypertension, and HE plus ME
was the most effective lifestyle intervention for reducing DBP. This study
underlines the importance of dietary factors and exercise in the man­
agement of prehypertension and highlights the superiority of multi-
component lifestyle interventions. Furthermore, tailored approaches
are essential to address the increasing burden of prehypertension in
different populations.
